text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
--Nordic countries are jointly to set up a weapons database to help fight warring bike gans and to investigate the gangs' finances.
--Leading members of the far-left Socialist Peoples' Party are in favour of approving the Amsterdam EU treaty when it is put to a referendum next year.

--Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft, seeking to prevent overheating in the burgeoning building industry, is seeking to curb public construction projects by imposing a levy of 20 percent of costs on other ministries who inititiate building projects.
--The big banks are expected to earn about one billion crowns handling the sale of the state's holding in Tele Danmark, expected next year.
--The far left and the right in parliament are critical of the government's plans to draft a 1998 budget that will appeal to both sides and say that the result may be that it is supported by neither.
--The Nordic Council has warned Denmark against its plans to impose a quota on Norwegians seeking to study in Denmark, saying that it would be a serious step backward for Nordic co-operation.
--Farm earnings rose in 1996 to 266,800 crowns per holding from 233,000 in 1995, but arable and cattle farmers' earnings dropped while pig producers accounted for all of the rise.

--Panicked at the losses incurred by cleaning group ISS' U.S. unit last year, many Danes sold their shares at around 120 crowns. Today only about a third of the shares are in Danish hands, compared with 75 percent a year ago and they are now worth about 250 crowns.

--Several overseas analysts believe that 1998 is not a good time to complete the privatisation of Tele Danmark, as a planned France Telecom selloff, is glutting the market and could force the Danish group's share price down in a sale.
